name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - Reaction of concentrated sulphuric acid with halides

questiontext.text: On addition of conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to a chloride salt, colourless fumes are evolved but in case of iodide salt, violet fumes come out. This is because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Concentrated sulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)) acts both as a strong acid and as a moderately strong oxidising agent. The reducing power of hydrogen halides (\(\mathrm{HX}\)) increases down the group in the order \(\mathrm{HF} < \mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{HBr} < \mathrm{HI}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
When conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) is added to a chloride salt, \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas is evolved as colourless fumes. Because \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is a weak reducing agent, it is not oxidised by conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\).

Step 3: Application
When conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) is added to an iodide salt, \(\mathrm{HI}\) is initially formed. However, \(\mathrm{HI}\) is a strong reducing agent and immediately reduces \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to \(\mathrm{SO}_2\), while \(\mathrm{HI}\) itself gets oxidised to \(\mathrm{I}_2\), which evolves as violet fumes:
\(2\mathrm{HI} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + \mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Violet fumes appear because \(\mathrm{HI}\) gets oxidised to \(\mathrm{I}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - Qualitative analysis of copper sulphide with ammonia

questiontext.text: In qualitative analysis when \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) is passed through an aqueous solution of salt acidified with dil. \(\mathrm{HCl}\), a black precipitate is obtained. On boiling the precipitate with dil. \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\), it forms a solution of blue colour. Addition of excess of aqueous solution of ammonia to this solution gives

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Group II qualitative analysis, passing \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) through an acidified solution precipitates \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions as black copper(II) sulphide (\(\mathrm{CuS}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
On boiling the black \(\mathrm{CuS}\) precipitate with dilute \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\), it dissolves to form a blue aqueous solution of copper(II) nitrate, \(\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2}\):
\(3\mathrm{CuS} + 8\mathrm{HNO}_3 \rightarrow 3\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2} + 2\mathrm{NO} + 3\mathrm{S} + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

Step 3: Application
When excess aqueous ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)) is added to the blue solution containing \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions, a soluble, intensely coloured tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion is formed:
\(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \left[\mathrm{Cu(NH_3)_4}\right]^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})\)

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Addition of excess aqueous ammonia produces a deep blue solution of \(\left[\mathrm{Cu}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{4}\right]^{2+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q03 - Single and double bonds in cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid

questiontext.text: In a cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid molecule, how many single and double bonds are present?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The molecule is cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid, which has the molecular formula \((\mathrm{HPO}_3)_3\) or \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{P}_3\mathrm{O}_9\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each phosphorus atom is pentavalent (forms 5 covalent bonds), oxygen is divalent, and hydrogen is monovalent.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid has a six-membered cyclic ring consisting of three alternating phosphorus atoms and three oxygen atoms connected by \(\mathrm{P-O-P}\) linkages. Each phosphorus atom is also bonded to one oxo group (\(=\mathrm{O}\)) and one hydroxyl group (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Count the double bonds:
Each of the 3 phosphorus atoms has one \(\mathrm{P=O}\) double bond, giving \(3\) double bonds.
Count the single bonds:
1. Ring \(\mathrm{P-O}\) single bonds: \(6\) single bonds (two per \(\mathrm{P}\) atom in the 6-membered ring).
2. Exocyclic \(\mathrm{P-O}\) single bonds to the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups: \(3\) single bonds (one per \(\mathrm{P}\) atom).
3. \(\mathrm{O-H}\) single bonds in the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups: \(3\) single bonds.
Total single bonds \(= 6 + 3 + 3 = 12\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Total valence bonds: \(3\) double bonds and \(12\) single bonds. Thus, cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid contains 3 double bonds and 12 single bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q04 - Element capable of p-pi d-pi bonding

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements can be involved in \(\mathrm{p}\pi\text{–}\mathrm{d}\pi\) bonding?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For an element to participate in \(\mathrm{p}\pi\text{–}\mathrm{d}\pi\) bonding, it must possess vacant \(d\)-orbitals of suitable energy in its valence shell.

Step 2: Evaluation
Boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)), carbon (\(\mathrm{C}\)), and nitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}\)) belong to the second period of the periodic table. Their valence shell is \(n = 2\), which contains only \(2s\) and \(2p\) orbitals and lacks \(d\)-orbitals.

Step 3: Application
Phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}\)) belongs to the third period (\(n = 3\)), so it has vacant \(3d\) orbitals available in its valence shell. Therefore, phosphorus can form \(\mathrm{p}\pi\text{–}\mathrm{d}\pi\) bonds (for example, with oxygen in \(\mathrm{PO}_4^{3-}\) or \(\mathrm{P}_4\mathrm{O}_{10}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Phosphorus can be involved in \(\mathrm{p}\pi\text{–}\mathrm{d}\pi\) bonding.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q05 - Isoelectronic and isostructural ion pairs

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs of ions are isoelectronic and isostructural?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The ions to be compared are \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\), \(\mathrm{NO}_3^{-}\), \(\mathrm{ClO}_3^{-}\), and \(\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Isoelectronic species have the same total number of electrons (or valence electrons). Isostructural species have the same hybridisation on the central atom and the same molecular geometry.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total electrons \(=\) sum of atomic numbers of all atoms \(+\) negative charge. Geometry is determined by VSEPR theory via steric number \(=\frac{1}{2}(V + M - C + A)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\):
Total electrons \(= 6 + 3(8) + 2 = 32\).
Central carbon atom has \(3\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(sp^2\) hybridised), giving a trigonal planar geometry.
For \(\mathrm{NO}_3^{-}\):
Total electrons \(= 7 + 3(8) + 1 = 32\).
Central nitrogen atom has \(3\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(sp^2\) hybridised), giving a trigonal planar geometry.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\) and \(\mathrm{NO}_3^{-}\) have \(32\) electrons and trigonal planar structure, so they are isoelectronic and isostructural.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q06 - Bond dissociation enthalpy of halogen acids

questiontext.text: Affinity for hydrogen decreases in the group from fluorine to iodine. Which of the halogen acids should have highest bond dissociation enthalpy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bond dissociation enthalpy of a covalent \(\mathrm{H-X}\) bond depends inversely on the bond length and directly on the extent of orbital overlap between hydrogen and the halogen atom.

Step 2: Evaluation
Moving down Group 17 from fluorine to iodine, the atomic size of the halogen increases. Consequently, the \(\mathrm{H-X}\) bond length increases in the order \(\mathrm{H-F} < \mathrm{H-Cl} < \mathrm{H-Br} < \mathrm{H-I}\).

Step 3: Application
Since fluorine is the smallest halogen, the \(1s\text{–}2p\) orbital overlap in \(\mathrm{HF}\) is the strongest and the \(\mathrm{H-F}\) bond is the shortest, requiring the maximum energy to break.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{HF}\) has the highest bond dissociation enthalpy among the halogen acids.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q07 - Reducing strength of group 15 hydrides

questiontext.text:
Bond dissociation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) (\(\mathrm{E} = \text{element}\)) bonds is given below. Which of the compounds will act as strongest reducing agent?

Compound\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)\(\mathrm{AsH}_3\)\(\mathrm{SbH}_3\)
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{diss}}(\mathrm{E\text{—}H})/\mathrm{kJ\,mol}^{-1}\)389322297255

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) bond dissociation enthalpies are: \(\mathrm{NH}_3 = 389\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{PH}_3 = 322\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{AsH}_3 = 297\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), and \(\mathrm{SbH}_3 = 255\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A hydride acts as a reducing agent by donating hydrogen atoms (or electrons) upon cleavage of the \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) bond.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Reducing character of hydrides is inversely proportional to the \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) bond dissociation enthalpy: the weaker the \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) bond, the more readily hydrogen is released, and the stronger the reducing agent.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the given values:
\(389 > 322 > 297 > 255\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\mathrm{SbH}_3\) has the lowest \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) bond dissociation enthalpy (\(255\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) because \(\mathrm{Sb}\) has the largest atomic size among the listed Group 15 elements, leading to the longest and weakest \(\mathrm{Sb\text{—}H}\) bond.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\mathrm{SbH}_3\) loses hydrogen most easily, \(\mathrm{SbH}_3\) acts as the strongest reducing agent.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q08 - Properties of phosphine gas from white phosphorus

questiontext.text: On heating with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution in an inert atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\), white phosphorus gives a gas. Which of the following statement is incorrect about the gas?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
White phosphorus reacts with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution in an inert atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) to produce phosphine gas (\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)):
\(\mathrm{P}_4 + 3\mathrm{NaOH} + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{PH}_3 + 3\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\)

Step 2: Evaluation
Phosphine (\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)) is a colourless, highly poisonous gas with a rotten fish smell, and its aqueous solution decomposes in the presence of light to give red phosphorus and \(\mathrm{H}_2\).

Step 3: Application
Comparing basicity, phosphorus is larger and less electronegative than nitrogen, and the lone pair on phosphorus in \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) resides in a more diffused \(s\)-rich orbital compared to the \(sp^3\) orbital in \(\mathrm{NH}_3\). Therefore, \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) is a much weaker base than \(\mathrm{NH}_3\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The statement that the gas is more basic than \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is incorrect.

answer.text: It is highly poisonous and has smell like rotten fish.
Its solution in water decomposes in the presence of light.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q09 - Tribasic acid forming three series of salts

questiontext.text: Which of the following acids forms three series of salts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The number of series of salts formed by an acid corresponds to its basicity, which for oxoacids of phosphorus equals the number of ionisable \(\mathrm{P-OH}\) groups.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) has one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group and two \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds, so it is monobasic (1 series of salts).
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{BO}_3\) is a weak monobasic Lewis acid (accepts one \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ion).
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\) has two \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups and one \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bond, so it is dibasic (2 series of salts).
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) (orthophosphoric acid) has three \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups attached to phosphorus and is tribasic.

Step 3: Application
Because \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) has three ionisable protons, it forms three series of salts: \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_4\), \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{HPO}_4\), and \(\mathrm{Na}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) forms three series of salts.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q10 - Cause of strong reducing behaviour of hypophosphorous acid

questiontext.text: Strong reducing behaviour of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) is due to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In oxoacids of phosphorus, the reducing property is governed by the presence of \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds directly attached to the phosphorus atom.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hypophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\), phosphinic acid) has a tetrahedral phosphorus centre bonded to one \(=\mathrm{O}\) atom, one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group, and two \(\mathrm{H}\) atoms.

Step 3: Application
The two \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds can be readily oxidised to \(\mathrm{P-OH}\) bonds, making \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) a strong reducing agent (for example, reducing \(\mathrm{AgNO}_3\) to metallic \(\mathrm{Ag}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The strong reducing behaviour of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) is due to the presence of one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group and two \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds.

answer.text: Presence of two \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups and one \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bond
Presence of one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group and two \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q11 - Thermal decomposition products of lead nitrate

questiontext.text: On heating lead nitrate forms oxides of nitrogen and lead. The oxides formed are

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Heavy metal nitrates decompose upon heating to give the metal oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide gas (\(\mathrm{NO}_2\)), and oxygen gas (\(\mathrm{O}_2\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Lead(II) nitrate undergoes thermal decomposition according to the balanced equation:
\(2\mathrm{Pb(NO_3)_2(s)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\mathrm{PbO(s)} + 4\mathrm{NO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + \mathrm{O}_2\mathrm{(g)}\)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The oxides formed are \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{PbO}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q12 - Allotropy in group 15 elements

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements does not show allotropy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Allotropy in Group 15 elements depends on the ability of the element to form catenated or polymeric single-bonded structures.

Step 2: Evaluation
Phosphorus, arsenic, antimony, and bismuth exhibit allotropy. Nitrogen, however, has a very small atomic size, which leads to high interelectronic repulsion between non-bonding lone pairs on adjacent nitrogen atoms in a single \(\mathrm{N-N}\) bond.

Step 3: Application
Because the \(\mathrm{N-N}\) single bond is very weak compared to the \(\mathrm{N\equiv N}\) triple bond, nitrogen exists exclusively as discrete diatomic \(\mathrm{N}_2\) molecules and does not form polymeric allotropes.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Nitrogen does not show allotropy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q13 - Maximum covalency of nitrogen

questiontext.text: Maximum covalency of nitrogen is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The maximum covalency of an element is limited by the total number of orbitals available in its valence shell for bonding.

Step 2: Evaluation
Nitrogen has the ground-state valence electronic configuration \(2s^2 2p^3\). Its valence shell (\(n = 2\)) has only one \(2s\) orbital and three \(2p\) orbitals, and no \(2d\) orbitals exist.

Step 3: Application
With four valence orbitals in total, nitrogen can form a maximum of four covalent bonds (for example, in \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\) or \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5\)), which restricts its maximum covalency to 4.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The maximum covalency of nitrogen is 4.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q14 - Incorrect statement about nitrogen and phosphorus compounds

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is wrong?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bond strength of single homonuclear bonds in second-period elements with lone pairs is weakened by interelectronic repulsion between lone pairs on adjacent small atoms.

Step 2: Evaluation
- In a single \(\mathrm{N-N}\) bond, the small size of nitrogen atoms causes strong lone-pair–lone-pair repulsion, making the \(\mathrm{N-N}\) single bond weaker than the \(\mathrm{P-P}\) single bond.
- \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) has a lone pair of electrons on phosphorus and can act as a ligand with transition metals.
- \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) has an odd number of electrons (one unpaired electron), making it paramagnetic.
- In \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5\), each nitrogen atom forms four covalent bonds (covalency is 4).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement that a single \(\mathrm{N-N}\) bond is stronger than a single \(\mathrm{P-P}\) bond is wrong.

answer.text: Single \(\mathrm{N-N}\) bond is stronger than the single \(\mathrm{P-P}\) bond.
\(\mathrm{PH}_3\) can act as a ligand in the formation of coordination compound with transition elements.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q15 - Brown ring test complex for nitrate ion

questiontext.text: A brown ring is formed in the ring test for \(\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) ion. It is due to the formation of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the brown ring test for nitrate ions (\(\mathrm{NO}_3^-\)), freshly prepared \(\mathrm{FeSO}_4\) solution reduces \(\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) to nitric oxide (\(\mathrm{NO}\)) in the presence of concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The reactions involved are:
\(\mathrm{NO}_3^- + 3\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} + 4\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow \mathrm{NO} + 3\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)
\(\left[\mathrm{Fe(H_2O)_6}\right]^{2+} + \mathrm{NO} \rightarrow \left[\mathrm{Fe(H_2O)_5(NO)}\right]^{2+} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The brown ring is due to the formation of the complex \(\left[\mathrm{Fe}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\right)_{5}(\mathrm{NO})\right]^{2+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q16 - Well characterised bismuth compound in +5 oxidation state

questiontext.text: Elements of group-15 form compounds in \(+5\) oxidation state. However, bismuth forms only one well characterised compound in \(+5\) oxidation state. The compound is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Due to the inert pair effect, the stability of the \(+5\) oxidation state decreases down Group 15, while the \(+3\) oxidation state becomes progressively more stable. Thus, \(\mathrm{Bi(V)}\) is a very strong oxidising agent.

Step 2: Evaluation
Only the most electronegative and smallest halogen, fluorine, can stabilise bismuth in its \(+5\) oxidation state by forming \(\mathrm{BiF}_5\). Less electronegative elements like chlorine, oxygen, or sulphur are oxidised by \(\mathrm{Bi(V)}\) and cannot form stable, well-characterised \(\mathrm{Bi(V)}\) compounds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The only well-characterised compound of bismuth in the \(+5\) oxidation state is \(\mathrm{BiF}_5\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q17 - Thermal decomposition of ammonium dichromate and barium azide

questiontext.text: On heating ammonium dichromate and barium azide separately we get

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both ammonium dichromate and metal azides undergo thermal decomposition to liberate dinitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}_2\)) gas.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. Thermal decomposition of ammonium dichromate:
\((\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{N}_2 + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)
2. Thermal decomposition of barium azide (gives very pure \(\mathrm{N}_2\)):
\(\mathrm{Ba(N_3)_2} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{Ba} + 3\mathrm{N}_2\)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Heating ammonium dichromate and barium azide separately yields \(\mathrm{N}_2\) in both cases.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q18 - Stoichiometry of catalytic oxidation of ammonia

questiontext.text: In the preparation of \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\), we get \(\mathrm{NO}\) gas by catalytic oxidation of ammonia. The moles of \(\mathrm{NO}\) produced by the oxidation of two moles of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) will be ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Moles of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) oxidised \(= 2\text{ mol}\). Process: catalytic oxidation of ammonia in Ostwald's process for \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) preparation.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Oxygen is present in excess so that ammonia undergoes complete catalytic oxidation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The balanced chemical equation for the catalytic oxidation of ammonia over a \(\mathrm{Pt/Rh}\) gauze catalyst at \(500\text{ K}\) and \(9\text{ bar}\) is:
\(4\mathrm{NH}_3\mathrm{(g)} + 5\mathrm{O}_2\mathrm{(g)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pt/Rh},\,500\text{ K},\,9\text{ bar}} 4\mathrm{NO(g)} + 6\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(g)}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
From the stoichiometry of the balanced equation, \(4\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) produce \(4\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NO}\).
Therefore, the molar ratio \(\mathrm{NH}_3 : \mathrm{NO} = 1 : 1\).
For \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\):
\(\text{Moles of NO} = 2\text{ mol}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Nitrogen atoms are conserved (\(2\text{ mol N}\) in \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) gives \(2\text{ mol N}\) in \(\mathrm{NO}\)). Thus, 2 moles of \(\mathrm{NO}\) are produced.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q19 - Oxidation state of phosphorus in sodium hypophosphite

questiontext.text: The oxidation state of central atom in the anion of compound \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\) will be ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The compound is \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\). Its anion is \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{PO}_2^-\), with central atom phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard oxidation numbers: \(\mathrm{H} = +1\) and \(\mathrm{O} = -2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The algebraic sum of oxidation numbers of all atoms in a polyatomic ion equals the net charge on the ion.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Let the oxidation state of \(\mathrm{P}\) in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{PO}_2^-\) be \(x\).
\(2(+1) + x + 2(-2) = -1\)
\(2 + x - 4 = -1\)
\(x - 2 = -1\)
\(x = +1\)

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking with the neutral salt \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\): \(+1 + 2(+1) + (+1) + 2(-2) = 0\). Thus, the oxidation state of phosphorus is \(+1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q20 - Identifying non-tetrahedral species

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not tetrahedral in shape?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molecular shape is determined by the number of bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom according to VSEPR theory.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\): Central \(\mathrm{N}\) has \(4\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(sp^3\)) \(\rightarrow\) tetrahedral.
- \(\mathrm{SiCl}_4\): Central \(\mathrm{Si}\) has \(4\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(sp^3\)) \(\rightarrow\) tetrahedral.
- \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\): Central \(\mathrm{S}\) has \(4\) \(\sigma\)-bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(sp^3\)) \(\rightarrow\) tetrahedral.
- \(\mathrm{SF}_4\): Central \(\mathrm{S}\) has \(6\) valence electrons; \(4\) are used in forming \(\mathrm{S-F}\) bonds and \(2\) remain as \(1\) lone pair. This gives a steric number of \(5\) (\(sp^3d\) hybridisation, trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry).

Step 3: Application
With \(4\) bond pairs and \(1\) lone pair in an equatorial position, \(\mathrm{SF}_4\) adopts a see-saw shape rather than a tetrahedral shape.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{SF}_4\) is not tetrahedral in shape.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q21 - Identifying peroxoacids of sulphur

questiontext.text: Which of the following are peroxoacids of sulphur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Peroxoacids of sulphur are oxoacids that contain at least one peroxo linkage (\(\mathrm{-O-O-}\)) in their structure.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_5\) (peroxomonosulphuric acid, Caro's acid) contains one \(\mathrm{-O-O-}\) linkage.
- \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_8\) (peroxodisulphuric acid, Marshall's acid) contains one \(\mathrm{-O-O-}\) linkage between the two sulphur-centred tetrahedral units.
- \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_7\) (pyrosulphuric acid or oleum) contains a \(\mathrm{S-O-S}\) oxide bridge, not a peroxo linkage.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_5\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_8\) are peroxoacids of sulphur.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q22 - Oxidation of carbon by hot concentrated sulphuric acid

questiontext.text: Hot conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) acts as moderately strong oxidising agent. It oxidises both metals and nonmetals. Which of the following element is oxidised by conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) into two gaseous products?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hot concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) oxidises metals and non-metals while itself being reduced to \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) gas.

Step 2: Evaluation
- Copper: \(\mathrm{Cu} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\text{conc.}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO}_4 + \mathrm{SO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (only one gaseous product, \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).
- Sulphur: \(\mathrm{S} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\text{conc.}) \rightarrow 3\mathrm{SO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (only one gaseous product, \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).
- Zinc: \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\text{conc.}) \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO}_4 + \mathrm{SO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (only one gaseous product, \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).
- Carbon: \(\mathrm{C} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\text{conc.}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + 2\mathrm{SO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (two gaseous products, \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Carbon (\(\mathrm{C}\)) is oxidised by hot conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) into two gaseous products (\(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q23 - Oxidation state change of nitrogen in reaction with excess chlorine

questiontext.text: A black compound of manganese reacts with a halogen acid to give greenish yellow gas. When excess of this gas reacts with \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) an unstable trihalide is formed. In this process the oxidation state of nitrogen changes from

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Manganese dioxide (\(\mathrm{MnO}_2\), a black compound) oxidises concentrated hydrochloric acid (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)) to liberate greenish-yellow chlorine gas (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2\)):
\(\mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnCl}_2 + \mathrm{Cl}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

Step 2: Evaluation
When excess \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\) reacts with \(\mathrm{NH}_3\), it forms the explosive, unstable nitrogen trichloride (\(\mathrm{NCl}_3\)):
\(\mathrm{NH}_3 + 3\mathrm{Cl}_2\text{ (excess)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NCl}_3 + 3\mathrm{HCl}\)

Step 3: Application
In \(\mathrm{NH}_3\), hydrogen has oxidation state \(+1\), so nitrogen has oxidation state \(-3\).
In \(\mathrm{NCl}_3\), chlorine is more electronegative than nitrogen and has oxidation state \(-1\), so nitrogen has oxidation state \(+3\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The oxidation state of nitrogen changes from \(-3\) to \(+3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q24 - Reason for Bartlett using O2+PtF6- for xenon compounds

questiontext.text: In the preparation of compounds of \(\mathrm{Xe}\), Bartlett had taken \(\mathrm{O}_2^+\,\mathrm{PtF}_6^-\) as a base compound. This is because

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q25 - Structure of phosphorus pentachloride in solid state

questiontext.text: In solid state \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) is a

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) exists as discrete trigonal bipyramidal molecules in the gaseous and liquid phases, it undergoes autoionisation in the solid state to achieve greater lattice stability.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the solid state, \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) exists as an ionic solid composed of \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_4\right]^+\) cations and \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_6\right]^-\) anions.

Step 3: Application

- In \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_6\right]^-\), phosphorus is \(sp^3d^2\) hybridised with \(6\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs, giving an octahedral geometry.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
In the solid state, \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) is an ionic solid with \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_4\right]^+\) tetrahedral and \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_6\right]^-\) octahedral.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q26 - Decreasing order of oxidising power from reduction potentials

questiontext.text:
Reduction potentials of some ions are given below. Arrange them in decreasing order of oxidising power.

Ion\(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-\)\(\mathrm{IO}_4^-\)\(\mathrm{BrO}_4^-\)
Reduction potential \(E^\circ/\mathrm{V}\)\(E^\circ = 1.19\,\mathrm{V}\)\(E^\circ = 1.65\,\mathrm{V}\)\(E^\circ = 1.74\,\mathrm{V}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard reduction potentials (\(E^\circ\)):
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-) = 1.19\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{IO}_4^-) = 1.65\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{BrO}_4^-) = 1.74\text{ V}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Higher (more positive) standard reduction potential indicates a greater tendency for the species to gain electrons (be reduced).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Oxidising power is directly proportional to the standard reduction potential (\(E^\circ\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Arranging the \(E^\circ\) values in decreasing order:
\(1.74\text{ V} > 1.65\text{ V} > 1.19\text{ V}\).
Correspondingly, the decreasing order of oxidising power is:
\(\mathrm{BrO}_4^- > \mathrm{IO}_4^- > \mathrm{ClO}_4^-\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(\mathrm{BrO}_4^-\) has the highest reduction potential and \(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-\) the lowest, so the decreasing order of oxidising power is \(\mathrm{BrO}_4^- > \mathrm{IO}_4^- > \mathrm{ClO}_4^-\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q27 - Identifying isoelectronic halogen and interhalogen species

questiontext.text: Which of the following is isoelectronic pair?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Atomic numbers: \(\mathrm{C} = 6\), \(\mathrm{N} = 7\), \(\mathrm{O} = 8\), \(\mathrm{F} = 9\), \(\mathrm{Cl} = 17\), \(\mathrm{Br} = 35\), \(\mathrm{I} = 53\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Isoelectronic species have the same total number of electrons.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Total electrons} = \sum Z_i - \text{charge}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- \(\mathrm{ICl}_2\) and \(\mathrm{ClO}_2\): \(53 + 2(17) = 87\) vs. \(17 + 2(8) = 33\) (not equal).
- \(\mathrm{BrO}_2^-\) and \(\mathrm{BrF}_2^+\):
\(\mathrm{BrO}_2^- = 35 + 2(8) + 1 = 52\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{BrF}_2^+ = 35 + 2(9) - 1 = 52\) electrons (equal).
- \(\mathrm{ClO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{BrF}\): \(17 + 2(8) = 33\) vs. \(35 + 9 = 44\) (not equal).
- \(\mathrm{CN}^-\) and \(\mathrm{O}_3\): \(6 + 7 + 1 = 14\) vs. \(3(8) = 24\) (not equal).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both \(\mathrm{BrO}_2^-\) and \(\mathrm{BrF}_2^+\) have \(52\) electrons (and \(20\) valence electrons), so \(\mathrm{BrO}_2^-, \mathrm{BrF}_2^+\) is an isoelectronic pair.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q28 - Disproportionation of chlorine in hot sodium hydroxide

questiontext.text: If chlorine gas is passed through hot \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution, two changes are observed in the oxidation number of chlorine during the reaction. These are ______ and ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When chlorine gas reacts with hot and concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution, it undergoes a disproportionation reaction, simultaneously getting reduced and oxidised.

Step 2: Evaluation
The balanced chemical equation is:
\(3\mathrm{Cl}_2 + 6\mathrm{NaOH}\text{ (hot, conc.)} \rightarrow 5\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{NaClO}_3 + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

Step 3: Application
- In \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\), the oxidation state of chlorine is \(0\).
- In \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), the oxidation state of chlorine is \(-1\) (reduction: \(0\) to \(-1\)).
- In \(\mathrm{NaClO}_3\), let the oxidation state of \(\mathrm{Cl}\) be \(x\): \(+1 + x + 3(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +5\) (oxidation: \(0\) to \(+5\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The two changes observed in the oxidation number of chlorine are \(0\) to \(+5\) and \(0\) to \(-1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q29 - Properties and trends of halogens and halides

questiontext.text: Which of the following options are not in accordance with the property mentioned against them?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Periodic trends among halogens and their compounds depend on standard reduction potentials, polarising power and polarisability (Fajans' rules), bond dissociation enthalpies, and atomic size.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Relation
1. Oxidising power: Standard reduction potentials decrease from fluorine to iodine, so the oxidising power follows \(\mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2\). This order is in accordance with the property.
2. Ionic character of metal halide: According to Fajans' rules, for a given metal cation \(\mathrm{M}^+\), a larger halide anion is more easily polarised, increasing covalent character and decreasing ionic character. Thus, ionic character follows \(\mathrm{MF} > \mathrm{MCl} > \mathrm{MBr} > \mathrm{MI}\). The stated order \(\mathrm{MI} > \mathrm{MBr} > \mathrm{MCl} > \mathrm{MF}\) is incorrect.
3. Bond dissociation enthalpy: Due to the very small size of fluorine atoms, strong inter-electronic repulsion between lone pairs weakens the \(\mathrm{F–F}\) bond compared to \(\mathrm{Cl–Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{Br–Br}\). The actual order is \(\mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2\). Thus, \(\mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2\) is incorrect.
4. Hydrogen–halogen bond strength: As halogen size increases from \(\mathrm{F}\) to \(\mathrm{I}\), the \(\mathrm{H–X}\) bond length increases and bond strength decreases, giving \(\mathrm{HI} < \mathrm{HBr} < \mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{HF}\). This order is in accordance with the property.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The relations not in accordance with the stated properties are \(\mathrm{MI} > \mathrm{MBr} > \mathrm{MCl} > \mathrm{MF}\) for ionic character of metal halides and \(\mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2\) for bond dissociation enthalpy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q30 - Structure and bonding in white phosphorus

questiontext.text: Which of the following is correct for \(\mathrm{P}_4\) molecule of white phosphorus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
White phosphorus consists of discrete tetrahedral \(\mathrm{P}_4\) molecules in which four phosphorus atoms occupy the four vertices of a regular tetrahedron.

Step 2: Evaluation of Bonding and Lone Pairs
Each phosphorus atom has five valence electrons (\(3s^2 3p^3\)). In the tetrahedral \(\mathrm{P}_4\) molecule, each phosphorus atom forms three single covalent \(\mathrm{P–P}\) bonds with the other three phosphorus atoms. Since a tetrahedron has 6 edges, there are six \(\mathrm{P–P}\) single bonds in total. Using three valence electrons in bonding leaves one lone pair of electrons on each of the four phosphorus atoms, giving a total of four lone pairs in the molecule.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The \(\mathrm{P}_4\) molecule of white phosphorus has six \(\mathrm{P–P}\) single bonds and four lone pairs of electrons.

answer.text: It has four lone pairs of electrons.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q31 - Properties of halogens and interhalogen compounds

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Interhalogen compounds (\(\mathrm{XX}'_n\)) are formed by the combination of halogens of different sizes and electronegativities. Their reactivity and maximum coordination number depend on the radius ratio \(r_{\mathrm{X}}/r_{\mathrm{X}'}\) and bond strengths.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
1. Radius ratio: Among stable halogens, iodine has the largest atomic radius and fluorine has the smallest atomic radius. Therefore, the radius ratio between iodine and fluorine is maximum.
2. Bond strength comparison: In general, the \(\mathrm{X–X}'\) covalent bond in interhalogen compounds is weaker than the \(\mathrm{X–X}\) bond in diatomic halogens (except the \(\mathrm{F–F}\) bond). Claiming that halogens (leaving \(\mathrm{F–F}\)) have a weaker \(\mathrm{X–X}\) bond than \(\mathrm{X–X}'\) is incorrect.
3. Maximum number of atoms: Because of the maximum radius ratio between iodine and fluorine, iodine forms \(\mathrm{IF}_7\), which has 8 atoms—the maximum number of atoms among all interhalogen compounds.
4. Reactivity: Due to the weaker \(\mathrm{X–X}'\) bond, interhalogen compounds are more reactive than halogens (except fluorine).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that the radius ratio between iodine and fluorine is maximum among halogens, the maximum number of atoms in interhalogen compounds is present in iodine fluoride (\(\mathrm{IF}_7\)), and interhalogen compounds are more reactive than halogen compounds.

answer.text: Among halogens, radius ratio between iodine and fluorine is maximum.
Leaving \(\mathrm{F—F}\) bond, all halogens have weaker \(\mathrm{X—X}\) bond than \(\mathrm{X—X}'\) bond in interhalogens.
Among interhalogen compounds maximum number of atoms are present in iodine fluoride.
Interhalogen compounds are more reactive than halogen compounds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q32 - Properties and structure of sulphur dioxide

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct for \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) gas?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sulphur dioxide (\(\mathrm{SO}_2\)) is an acidic oxide of sulphur with \(sp^2\) hybridised central sulphur, possessing reducing and disinfecting properties.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
1. Bleaching action: In the presence of moisture, \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) acts as a reducing bleaching agent (\(\mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 + 2[\mathrm{H}]\)). Thus, it acts as a bleaching agent in moist conditions.
2. Geometry: The sulphur atom in \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) has two bond pairs and one lone pair, giving it an angular (bent) geometry with a bond angle of about \(119.5^\circ\), not linear.
3. Disinfectant use: Dilute aqueous \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) is used as a disinfectant and preservative.
4. Preparation: \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) is prepared in the laboratory by treating a metal sulphite with dilute \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\), whereas treating a metal sulphide with dilute \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) produces \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) gas.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements for \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) gas are that it acts as a bleaching agent in moist conditions and its dilute solution is used as a disinfectant.

answer.text: It acts as bleaching agent in moist conditions.
It's dilute solution is used as disinfectant.
It can be prepared by the reaction of dilute \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) with metal sulphide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q33 - Bonding and structure of p-block compounds

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molecular geometry, resonance, angular strain, and solid-state ionic structures determine the bond lengths and reactivity of \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\), \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\), and \(\mathrm{P}_4\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
1. Bond lengths in \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\): In nitric acid, the \(\mathrm{N–OH}\) single bond is longer (\(140.6\text{ pm}\)) than the two equivalent resonating \(\mathrm{N–O}\) bonds (\(121\text{ pm}\)). Hence, all three \(\mathrm{N–O}\) bond lengths are not equal.
2. Bond lengths in gaseous \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\): Gaseous \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) has a trigonal bipyramidal geometry where the two axial \(\mathrm{P–Cl}\) bonds (\(240\text{ pm}\)) are longer than the three equatorial \(\mathrm{P–Cl}\) bonds (\(202\text{ pm}\)) due to greater axial-equatorial repulsion.
3. Reactivity of white phosphorus: In the tetrahedral \(\mathrm{P}_4\) molecule, the \(\mathrm{P–P–P}\) bond angle is \(60^\circ\), which introduces considerable angular strain and makes white phosphorus highly reactive.
4. Solid-state \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\): In the solid state, \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) exists as an ionic solid \([\mathrm{PCl}_4]^+[\mathrm{PCl}_6]^-\), in which the cation \([\mathrm{PCl}_4]^+\) is tetrahedral and the anion \([\mathrm{PCl}_6]^-\) is octahedral.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that the \(\mathrm{P}_4\) molecule in white phosphorus has angular strain making it very reactive, and solid \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) is ionic with a tetrahedral cation and an octahedral anion.

answer.text: All the three \(\mathrm{N–O}\) bond lengths in \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) are equal.
All \(\mathrm{P—Cl}\) bond lengths in \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) molecule in gaseous state are equal.
\(\mathrm{P}_4\) molecule in white phosphorus have angular strain therefore white phosphorus is very reactive.
\(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) is ionic in solid state in which cation is tetrahedral and anion is octahedral.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q34 - Periodic trends in p-block oxides and hydrides

questiontext.text: Which of the following orders are correct as per the properties mentioned against each?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Acidic strength of oxides increases with non-metallic character and electronegativity of the central element. Enthalpy of vaporisation depends on intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonding and van der Waals forces). Electron gain enthalpy depends on atomic size and inter-electronic repulsion. Thermal stability of hydrides depends on the \(\mathrm{E–H}\) bond dissociation enthalpy.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Order
1. Acid strength: Non-metallic character increases in the order \(\mathrm{As} < \mathrm{Si} < \mathrm{P} < \mathrm{S}\), so the acidic strength of the oxides increases as \(\mathrm{As}_2\mathrm{O}_3 < \mathrm{SiO}_2 < \mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{O}_3 < \mathrm{SO}_2\). This order is correct.
2. Enthalpy of vaporisation: Among Group 15 hydrides, \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) has the highest enthalpy of vaporisation due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding, while \(\mathrm{AsH}_3\) has stronger van der Waals forces than \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) due to higher molar mass. The correct order is \(\mathrm{PH}_3 < \mathrm{AsH}_3 < \mathrm{NH}_3\), so \(\mathrm{AsH}_3 < \mathrm{PH}_3 < \mathrm{NH}_3\) is incorrect.
3. More negative electron gain enthalpy: Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine, and sulphur has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than oxygen, because of compact \(2p\) orbitals in \(\mathrm{F}\) and \(\mathrm{O}\) causing greater inter-electronic repulsion. The correct order is \(\mathrm{O} < \mathrm{S} < \mathrm{F} < \mathrm{Cl}\).
4. Thermal stability: Down Group 16, atomic size increases, the \(\mathrm{E–H}\) bond length increases, and bond dissociation enthalpy decreases. Thus, thermal stability decreases in the order \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S} > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{Se} > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{Te}\). This order is correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct orders are \(\mathrm{As}_2\mathrm{O}_3 < \mathrm{SiO}_2 < \mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{O}_3 < \mathrm{SO}_2\) for acid strength and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S} > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{Se} > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{Te}\) for thermal stability.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q35 - Oxoacids of sulphur and industrial processes

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Oxoacids of sulphur contain characteristic \(\mathrm{S–S}\), \(\mathrm{S–O–S}\), or \(\mathrm{S–O–O–S}\) linkages, and the oxidation state of sulphur is determined from its bonding environment. Industrial processes such as the Haber's process and Contact process involve specific catalysts and enthalpy changes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
1. Structure of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_6\): Dithionic acid (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_6\)) has the structure \(\mathrm{HO–SO_2–SO_2–OH}\), which contains a direct \(\mathrm{S–S}\) bond. This statement is correct.
2. Oxidation state in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_5\): Peroxomonosulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_5\)) contains one peroxo linkage (\(\mathrm{–O–O–}\)) where the two oxygen atoms each have an oxidation state of \(-1\), while the remaining three oxygen atoms are at \(-2\). Thus, \(2(+1) + x + 3(-2) + 2(-1) = 0 \implies x = +6\). Sulphur is in the \(+6\) oxidation state.
3. Haber's process catalyst: In Haber's process for \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) synthesis, iron oxide with small amounts of \(\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\) (or finely divided iron with molybdenum as promoter) is used, not iron powder along with \(\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\) and \(\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{O}\).
4. Enthalpy change in \(\mathrm{SO}_3\) preparation: The catalytic oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) to \(\mathrm{SO}_3\) (\(2\mathrm{SO}_2 + \mathrm{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO}_3\)) is exothermic, with \(\Delta_r H^\circ = -196.6\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), so the change in enthalpy is negative, not positive.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that an \(\mathrm{S–S}\) bond is present in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_6\), and in peroxosulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_5\)) sulphur is in the \(+6\) oxidation state.

answer.text: In peroxosulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_5\)) sulphur is in \(+6\) oxidation state.
Iron powder along with \(\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\) and \(\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{O}\) is used as a catalyst in the preparation of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) by Haber's process.
Change in enthalpy is positive for the preparation of \(\mathrm{SO}_3\) by catalytic oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q36 - Oxidising action of concentrated sulphuric acid

questiontext.text: In which of the following reactions conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) is used as an oxidising reagent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An oxidising reagent undergoes reduction (a decrease in oxidation state) while causing another species to be oxidised (an increase in oxidation state). In \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\), sulphur is in the \(+6\) oxidation state.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Reaction
1. \(\mathrm{CaF}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \longrightarrow \mathrm{CaSO}_4 + 2\mathrm{HF}\): There is no change in the oxidation state of any element (\(\mathrm{S}\) remains \(+6\), \(\mathrm{F}\) remains \(-1\)). This is a non-redox acid-displacement reaction.
2. \(2\mathrm{HI} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \longrightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + \mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\): Iodine is oxidised from \(-1\) in \(\mathrm{HI}\) to \(0\) in \(\mathrm{I}_2\), while sulphur is reduced from \(+6\) in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to \(+4\) in \(\mathrm{SO}_2\). Thus, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) acts as an oxidising agent.
3. \(\mathrm{Cu} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \longrightarrow \mathrm{CuSO}_4 + \mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\): Copper is oxidised from \(0\) to \(+2\) in \(\mathrm{CuSO}_4\), while sulphur is reduced from \(+6\) in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to \(+4\) in \(\mathrm{SO}_2\). Thus, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) acts as an oxidising agent.
4. \(\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \longrightarrow \mathrm{NaHSO}_4 + \mathrm{HCl}\): There is no change in the oxidation state of any element (\(\mathrm{S}\) remains \(+6\), \(\mathrm{Cl}\) remains \(-1\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) acts as an oxidising reagent in the reactions \(2\mathrm{HI} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \longrightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + \mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \longrightarrow \mathrm{CuSO}_4 + \mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q37 - Properties of noble gases and xenon fluorides

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Noble gases are monoatomic with completely filled valence shells, so their interatomic interactions are purely weak dispersion forces. Xenon forms reactive fluorides whose hydrolysis behaviour depends on the oxidation state of xenon.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
1. Interatomic interactions: Being monoatomic and non-polar with stable closed-shell configurations, the only type of interactions between particles of noble gases are weak London dispersion forces.
2. Ionisation enthalpy: The first ionisation enthalpy of molecular oxygen (\(1175\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) is very close to that of xenon (\(1170\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), which led Neil Bartlett to synthesise the first noble gas compound \(\mathrm{Xe}^+[\mathrm{PtF}_6]^-\).
3. Hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\): Complete hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\) gives \(\mathrm{XeO}_3\) and \(\mathrm{HF}\) (\(\mathrm{XeF}_6 + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{XeO}_3 + 6\mathrm{HF}\)). Since xenon remains in the \(+6\) oxidation state, this is not a redox reaction.
4. Reactivity of xenon fluorides: Xenon fluorides (\(\mathrm{XeF}_2\), \(\mathrm{XeF}_4\), \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\)) are reactive strong fluorinating and oxidising agents.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The true statements are that the only type of interactions between particles of noble gases are due to weak dispersion forces, and the ionisation enthalpy of molecular oxygen is very close to that of xenon.

answer.text: Only type of interactions between particles of noble gases are due to weak dispersion forces.
Ionisation enthalpy of molecular oxygen is very close to that of xenon.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MATCHING_Q59 - Hybridisation and shape of xenon compounds

questiontext.text: Match the compounds given in Column I with the hybridisation and shape given in Column II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Using VSEPR theory, the steric number of the central xenon atom (number of \(\sigma\)-bond pairs plus lone pairs) determines its hybridisation and molecular geometry.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Compound
1. \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\): Xenon has 8 valence electrons; 6 form \(\sigma\)-bonds with fluorine and 1 remains as a lone pair (steric number \(= 7\)), giving \(sp^3d^3\) hybridisation and a distorted octahedral shape.
2. \(\mathrm{XeO}_3\): Xenon forms 3 \(\sigma\)-bonds (and 3 \(\pi\)-bonds) with oxygen and has 1 lone pair (steric number \(= 4\)), giving \(sp^3\) hybridisation and a pyramidal shape.
3. \(\mathrm{XeOF}_4\): Xenon forms 5 \(\sigma\)-bonds (4 with \(\mathrm{F}\) and 1 with \(\mathrm{O}\)) and has 1 lone pair (steric number \(= 6\)), giving \(sp^3d^2\) hybridisation and a square pyramidal shape.
4. \(\mathrm{XeF}_4\): Xenon forms 4 \(\sigma\)-bonds with fluorine and has 2 lone pairs (steric number \(= 6\)), giving \(sp^3d^2\) hybridisation and a square planar shape.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{XeF}_6\) corresponds to \(sp^3d^3\) - distorted octahedral, \(\mathrm{XeO}_3\) corresponds to \(sp^3\) - pyramidal, \(\mathrm{XeOF}_4\) corresponds to \(sp^3d^2\) - square pyramidal, and \(\mathrm{XeF}_4\) corresponds to \(sp^3d^2\) - square planar.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MATCHING_Q60 - Classification of metal and non-metal oxides

questiontext.text: Match the formulas of oxides given in Column I with the type of oxide given in Column II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Oxides are classified as acidic, basic, amphoteric, neutral, or mixed oxides based on their acid-base behaviour and the oxidation states of the central element.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Oxide
1. \(\mathrm{Pb}_3\mathrm{O}_4\): Red lead is a stoichiometric combination of \(\mathrm{PbO}\) and \(\mathrm{PbO}_2\) (\(2\mathrm{PbO}\cdot\mathrm{PbO}_2\)), containing lead in \(+2\) and \(+4\) oxidation states; hence it is a mixed oxide.
2. \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}\): Nitrous oxide does not react with acids or bases to form salts; hence it is a neutral oxide.
3. \(\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_7\): Manganese is in its highest \(+7\) oxidation state; high-oxidation-state transition metal oxides are covalent and acidic (forming \(\mathrm{HMnO}_4\) with water). Hence it is an acidic oxide.
4. \(\mathrm{Bi}_2\mathrm{O}_3\): Bismuth is the heaviest and most metallic element of Group 15, so its trioxide \(\mathrm{Bi}_2\mathrm{O}_3\) is a basic oxide.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{Pb}_3\mathrm{O}_4\) is a mixed oxide, \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}\) is a neutral oxide, \(\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_7\) is an acidic oxide, and \(\mathrm{Bi}_2\mathrm{O}_3\) is a basic oxide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MATCHING_Q61 - Uses and properties of p-block substances

questiontext.text: Match the items of Columns I and II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each \(p\)-block element or compound has characteristic chemical properties or industrial applications.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Item
1. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\): Sulphuric acid is used as the electrolyte in lead storage batteries.
2. \(\mathrm{CCl}_3\mathrm{NO}_2\): Chloropicrin (\(\mathrm{CCl}_3\mathrm{NO}_2\)) is a well-known tear gas.
3. \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\): Chlorine has the highest (most negative) electron gain enthalpy among all elements in the periodic table.
4. Sulphur: Group 16 elements (oxygen family) are called chalcogens (ore-forming elements), so sulphur is a chalcogen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) matches storage batteries, \(\mathrm{CCl}_3\mathrm{NO}_2\) matches tear gas, \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\) matches highest electron gain enthalpy, and sulphur matches chalcogen.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MATCHING_Q62 - Molecular shapes of p-block species

questiontext.text: Match the species given in Column I with the shape given in Column II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to VSEPR theory, the molecular shape is determined by the number of bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
1. \(\mathrm{SF}_4\): Sulphur has 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (\(sp^3d\) hybridisation), giving a see-saw shape.
2. \(\mathrm{BrF}_3\): Bromine has 3 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs (\(sp^3d\) hybridisation), giving a bent T-shape.
3. \(\mathrm{BrO}_3^-\): Bromine has 3 \(\sigma\)-bond pairs and 1 lone pair (\(sp^3\) hybridisation), giving a pyramidal shape.
4. \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\): Nitrogen has 4 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs (\(sp^3\) hybridisation), giving a tetrahedral shape.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{SF}_4\) is see-saw shaped, \(\mathrm{BrF}_3\) is bent T-shaped, \(\mathrm{BrO}_3^-\) is pyramidal, and \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\) is tetrahedral.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MATCHING_Q63 - Noble gases and xenon fluorides

questiontext.text: Match the items of Columns I and II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Noble gases have specific technological uses based on their inertness and low solubility, while xenon fluorides differ in their hybridisation and hydrolysis behaviour.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Item
1. Partial hydrolysis without change in oxidation state: \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\) undergoes partial hydrolysis (\(\mathrm{XeF}_6 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{XeOF}_4 + 2\mathrm{HF}\)) where xenon remains in the \(+6\) oxidation state. (In contrast, \(\mathrm{XeF}_4\) disproportionates on hydrolysis).
2. Modern diving apparatus: Helium (\(\mathrm{He}\)) is used as a diluent for oxygen in modern diving apparatus because of its very low solubility in blood.
3. Inert atmosphere for electrical bulbs: Argon (\(\mathrm{Ar}\)) is used to provide an inert atmosphere for filling electrical bulbs.
4. Central atom in \(sp^3d^2\) hybridisation: In \(\mathrm{XeF}_4\), xenon has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs (steric number \(= 6\)), corresponding to \(sp^3d^2\) hybridisation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Partial hydrolysis without changing the central atom's oxidation state matches \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\), use in modern diving apparatus matches \(\mathrm{He}\), inert atmosphere in electrical bulbs matches \(\mathrm{Ar}\), and \(sp^3d^2\) hybridisation matches \(\mathrm{XeF}_4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_ASSERTIONREASON_Q64 - Reactivity of dinitrogen versus white phosphorus

questiontext.text:
Assertion : \(\mathrm{N}_2\) is less reactive than \(\mathrm{P}_4\).

Reason : Nitrogen has more electron gain enthalpy than phosphorus.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The chemical reactivity of \(\mathrm{N}_2\) compared to \(\mathrm{P}_4\) is governed by bond dissociation enthalpy and angular strain, whereas electron gain enthalpy depends on atomic size and inter-electronic repulsion.

Step 2: Evaluation of Assertion and Reason
1. Assertion: \(\mathrm{N}_2\) contains a very strong triple bond (\(\mathrm{N\equiv N}\)) with a high bond dissociation enthalpy (\(941.4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), making it inert at room temperature, whereas \(\mathrm{P}_4\) has weaker \(\mathrm{P–P}\) single bonds and significant angular strain (\(60^\circ\) bond angle). Thus, \(\mathrm{N}_2\) is less reactive than \(\mathrm{P}_4\), and the assertion is correct.
2. Reason: Due to the small size of the nitrogen atom and high electron density in its compact \(2p\) orbitals, an incoming electron experiences greater inter-electronic repulsion than in phosphorus. Consequently, nitrogen has a less negative (smaller) electron gain enthalpy than phosphorus. Thus, the reason statement is wrong.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion is a correct statement, whereas the reason is a wrong statement.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_ASSERTIONREASON_Q66 - Preparation of hydrogen iodide with concentrated sulphuric acid

questiontext.text:
Assertion : \(\mathrm{HI}\) cannot be prepared by the reaction of \(\mathrm{KI}\) with concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)

Reason : \(\mathrm{HI}\) has lowest \(\mathrm{H–X}\) bond strength among halogen acids.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) is a strong oxidising agent, whereas \(\mathrm{HI}\) is a strong reducing agent. Meanwhile, the bond strength of hydrogen halides (\(\mathrm{H–X}\)) depends on atomic size and bond length.

Step 2: Evaluation of Assertion and Reason
1. Assertion: When \(\mathrm{KI}\) is treated with concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\), the \(\mathrm{HI}\) initially formed is immediately oxidised by concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to \(\mathrm{I}_2\) (\(2\mathrm{HI} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + \mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)). Therefore, \(\mathrm{HI}\) cannot be prepared by this method, and the assertion is correct.
2. Reason: Down Group 17, the atomic radius of the halogen increases from \(\mathrm{F}\) to \(\mathrm{I}\), so the \(\mathrm{H–I}\) bond is the longest and has the lowest \(\mathrm{H–X}\) bond strength among the halogen acids (\(\mathrm{HF} > \mathrm{HCl} > \mathrm{HBr} > \mathrm{HI}\)). Thus, the reason statement is also correct, though the inability to prepare \(\mathrm{HI}\) using concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) is due to the oxidising nature of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) rather than the \(\mathrm{H–I}\) bond strength alone.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct statements, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_ASSERTIONREASON_Q67 - Atomicity of oxygen versus sulphur

questiontext.text:
Assertion : Both rhombic and monoclinic sulphur exist as \(\mathrm{S}_8\) but oxygen exists as \(\mathrm{O}_2\).

Reason : Oxygen forms \(p\pi - p\pi\) multiple bond due to small size and small bond length but \(p\pi - p\pi\) bonding is not possible in sulphur.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The ability of Group 16 elements to form \(p\pi - p\pi\) multiple bonds versus single-bonded polyatomic rings depends on atomic size and orbital overlap efficiency.

Step 2: Evaluation of Assertion and Reason
1. Assertion: Oxygen exists as a diatomic molecule (\(\mathrm{O}_2\)), whereas both rhombic and monoclinic allotropes of sulphur exist as puckered eight-membered \(\mathrm{S}_8\) rings. Thus, the assertion is correct.
2. Reason: Due to its small atomic size and short bond length, oxygen exhibits effective sideways overlap of \(2p\) orbitals to form a strong \(p\pi - p\pi\) double bond (\(\mathrm{O=O}\)). In contrast, sulphur has a larger atomic size and longer bond length, so \(p\pi - p\pi\) overlap is ineffective; instead, sulphur forms strong \(\mathrm{S–S}\) single bonds in an \(\mathrm{S}_8\) ring. Thus, the reason is correct and directly explains the assertion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct statements, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_ASSERTIONREASON_Q69 - Hydrolysis of sulphur hexafluoride versus sulphur tetrafluoride

questiontext.text:
Assertion : \(\mathrm{SF}_6\) cannot be hydrolysed but \(\mathrm{SF}_4\) can be.

Reason : Six \(\mathrm{F}\) atoms in \(\mathrm{SF}_6\) prevent the attack of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on sulphur atom of \(\mathrm{SF}_6\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydrolysis of covalent halides proceeds via nucleophilic attack by \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the central atom, which requires steric accessibility.

Step 2: Evaluation of Assertion and Reason
1. Assertion: \(\mathrm{SF}_6\) is kinetically inert towards hydrolysis by water, whereas \(\mathrm{SF}_4\) readily undergoes hydrolysis (\(\mathrm{SF}_4 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO}_2 + 4\mathrm{HF}\)). Thus, the assertion is correct.
2. Reason: In octahedral \(\mathrm{SF}_6\), the central sulphur atom is sterically shielded by six tightly packed fluorine atoms, preventing nucleophilic attack by \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecules. In contrast, see-saw shaped \(\mathrm{SF}_4\) has an accessible coordination site for water to attack. Thus, the reason is correct and explains the assertion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct statements, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
